extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (agents/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications on novelty, nonobviousness, inventorship, and specification requirements (written description, enablement, best mode), including rules for AIA vs pre-AIA applicability and special guidance for computer-implemented inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Naming of Inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent laws require naming the actual inventor or joint inventors of the claimed subject matter; an application must include or be amended to include the name of the inventor for any invention claimed (35 U.S.C. 115(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office presumes the named inventors are the actual inventors. Where an application names incorrect inventorship, applicant should submit a request to correct inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48 (see MPEP § 602.01(c) et seq.). In rare situations where it is clear the application does not name the correct inventorship and no request to correct has been filed, Office personnel should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 115. Do not use pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) rejections if the application is subject to first inventor to file (FITF) AIA provisions; consult MPEP § 2159 et seq. and MPEP § 2137 for pre-AIA 102(f) information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness Determination Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 sets forth the nonobviousness requirement, with important differences from pre-AIA law: obviousness is determined as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention and requires consideration of 'the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the effective filing date (not invention date) to determine obviousness for AIA-subject applications. The term 'claims' has long defined the invention; thus differences should be ascertained at the claim level (Graham factors). Continue to follow MPEP § 2141 et seq. and KSR guidance in formulating rationales to support conclusions of obviousness. Pre-AIA provisions like 103(b) and 103(c) differ and may be rare or replaced by AIA 102(b)(2)(C) and 102(c); consult MPEP § 2158 for distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art for Purposes of 103 (Use and Treatment of Disclosures)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 defines prior art for both novelty (102) and obviousness (103). A reference that is prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or (a)(2) and not excepted under 102(b) may be applied in an obviousness rejection under 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A non-enabling disclosure is prior art 'for all it teaches' for obviousness purposes (i.e., even if it cannot anticipate under 102 because it is non-enabling, it can be relied upon under 103 to show what it teaches). Examiners should determine whether a document qualifies as prior art under 102(a)(1) or (a)(2) and whether exceptions under 102(b) apply. Follow guidance and case law (e.g., Symbol Techs., Beckman Instruments) and MPEP § 2141 for formulating obviousness rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of AIA vs Pre-AIA 102/103 (Determining Effective Filing Date Status)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA changes to 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 apply only to applications (or claims) having an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013; determining whether an application/claim is subject to AIA or pre-AIA provisions is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application is an 'AIA application' if it contains or ever contained a claim with an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, or claims the benefit of an earlier application that ever contained such a claim. If even a single claim ever had such an effective filing date, AIA 102 and 103 apply to all claimed inventions in the application (even if claims with post-March 16, 2013 effective dates are later canceled). Applications filed before March 16, 2013 remain governed by pre-AIA law. Adding claims after March 16, 2013 that introduce new matter does not make a pre-March 16 application subject to AIA (35 U.S.C. 132(a) prohibits new matter). See MPEP §§ 2159-2159.03 for rules about transition applications and priority/benefit claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Amendments That Contain New Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 132(a) prohibits introduction of new matter into the disclosure; amendments believed to contain new matter must be treated to avoid improperly changing an application's applicable law status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner discovers a new drawing contains new matter, do not enter the drawing (MPEP § 608.02). Amendments to the written description or claims involving new matter are ordinarily entered, but the new matter must be canceled from the written description and claims directed to new matter rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (MPEP § 608.04). This process is administrative to handle alleged new matter and disputes between applicant and examiner. An amendment that would add a claim directed to new matter does not make a pre-AIA application into an AIA application for purposes of determining AIA applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification Three Separate Requirements (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / Pre-AIA 112, First Paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must include (A) a written description of the invention; (B) the manner and process of making and using the invention (enablement); and (C) the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out the invention (35 U.S.C. 112(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three requirements are separate and distinct. The written description is not the same as enablement; best mode is separate as well. See Ariad, Vas-Cath, and other cases cited. Examiners must consider each requirement independently when evaluating the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention as of the filing date (written description separate from enablement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession can be shown by showing species, embodiments, or sufficient descriptive detail. Generic or functional claim language in the original disclosure may fail written description if it does not support the claimed genus or scope (genus claims using functional language need sufficient species to show possession). Examples and case law (Ariad, LizardTech, Enzo Biochem, Fiers, Regents of Univ. of Cal.) illustrate failures: describing only one embodiment or merely reciting functions may not demonstrate possession of a broader invention. For computer-implemented functional claims, the specification must disclose the computer/algorithm/steps/flowcharts that perform the claimed function in sufficient detail; simply asserting that one skilled in the art could write a program is not enough. If inadequate, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112, first paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation (enablement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the In re Wands factors (weigh factual considerations) to decide whether undue experimentation is required: (1) breadth of the claims; (2) nature of the invention; (3) state of the prior art; (4) level of ordinary skill in the art; (5) level of predictability in the art; (6) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (7) existence of working examples; (8) quantity of experimentation needed. The undue experimentation determination is a conclusion reached by weighing these factors. See In re Wright, In re Wands, and MPEP § 2161 for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Mode Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must disclose the best mode of carrying out the claimed invention contemplated by the inventor at the time of filing; inquiry includes subjective knowledge of a best mode and objective adequacy of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine whether the inventor actually knew a best mode at filing (subjective). If so, determine whether the best mode was disclosed in sufficient detail to allow one skilled in the art to practice it (objective). Evidence of concealment (accidental or intentional) bears on best mode adequacy; only poor-quality disclosure that effectively conceals the best mode supports a best mode rejection. For software, best mode is generally satisfied by disclosure of software functions (writing code is typically within the skill of the art); flowcharts or source code are not generally required. See Fonar, Chemcast, and MPEP §§ 2165-2165.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description for Computer-Implemented Functional Claim Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented inventions claiming functionality, the written description must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail to show possession — including disclosure of the computer and the algorithm (or necessary steps/flowcharts) that perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claim language or a desired result is insufficient where the specification does not explain how the function is performed. Genus/functionally-defined claims are especially problematic if the specification does not describe species that achieve the claimed result. The specification must convey to a person skilled in the art that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter. For software claims, merely asserting that one skilled in the art could write a program to achieve the function is not enough — the specification should disclose how the inventor intended the function to be performed. If the specification fails to disclose sufficient algorithmic detail or corresponding structure for functional limitations, a 35 U.S.C. 112(a) written description rejection is appropriate; for means-plus-function limitations, lack of corresponding structure/materials/acts may require a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement for Computer-Implemented Functional Claim Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy enablement for computer-implemented functional limitations, the specification must teach how to make and use the full scope of the claimed function without undue experimentation, considering the interrelationship of hardware and software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the disclosure of hardware and software reasonably conveys possession and enables the full scope claimed. Consider the Wands factors, the nature and predictability of the technology, the amount of direction provided, existence of working examples, and whether undue experimentation would be needed. If the specification does not disclose sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts to perform the entire claimed function of a means-(or step-)plus-function limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA sixth paragraph), then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA second paragraph) must be made in addition to written description rejection (In re Donaldson). See MPEP §§ 2163-2163.07(b) and 2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus/Functional Claim Pitfall (Original Claims May Lack Written Description Support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original claims often fail written description when claim language is generic or functional (e.g., claiming a genus using functional language without describing sufficient species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate written description of a claimed genus requires more than a generic statement of the invention’s boundaries; the specification must demonstrate that the applicant invented species sufficient to support the functionally-defined genus. Cases such as Ariad, LizardTech, and Enzo Biochem illustrate that describing only one embodiment or restating desired results without describing how to achieve them may be insufficient. Examiners should look for support in the original disclosure that reasonably conveys possession of the claimed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-Plus-Function / Step-Plus-Function Requirements (35 U.S.C. 112(f) / Pre-AIA Sixth Paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims with means- (or step-) plus-function limitations require sufficient disclosure of corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the claimed function; failing to provide this corresponding disclosure can lead to rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA second paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification does not provide sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts for the full scope of a means- or step-plus-function limitation, the applicant has failed to 'particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention' as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Make a 112(b) rejection in addition to any written description rejection. See In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181 for means/step-plus-function guidance.
